## Part 1: Restaurant Health Inspections (25 points)

The first dataset contains restaurant health inspection scores from Montgomery County. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/montco_inspections.csv`

The dataset includes the name of the establishment, the number of points for critical and non-critical areas, the total points, maximum points possible, the compliance score, and the grade.

### Task 1: Read the data (2 points)

```{r}
InspScores <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/montco_inspections.csv")
```

### Task 2: Calculate the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of compliance scores. Save the results in a new dataframe called `compliance_stats`. (6 points)

```{r}
compliance_stats <- InspScores |> 
  mutate(
    mean_score = mean(compliance_score),
    sd_score = sd(compliance_score),
    z_score = (compliance_score - mean_score) / sd_score)
  
```

### Task 3: Create a histogram of the compliance scores with a vertical line showing the mean. Include a headline and label the x and y axes. (8 points)

```{r}
compliance_stats |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_histogram(aes(x = compliance_score), binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(compliance_score)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) 

 theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Compliance Scores",
       x = "Compliance Scores",
       y = "Count",
       caption = "Red dotted line = mean")
```

### Task 4: Write 2–3 sentences interpreting what the standard deviation and histogram tell us about the distribution of compliance scores. What would be newsworthy about this distribution? What's the story here? (9 points)

The standard deviation and histogram tell us that the distribution is clearly not normal. The sd being around .63 tells us that it doesn't follow the 68/95/99.7 rule, and the histogram shows us that the distribution is clearly skewed to the left. This happens naturally when there is a large cluster of values at the maximum of the data set.

## Part 2: Daily Transit Ridership — Z-Scores (30 points)

Your editor wants you to identify unusual days in WMATA's daily ridership data that might be worth investigating as story leads. The dataset contains daily bus and rail totals, along with the day of the week. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/wmata_daily.csv`

### Task 5: Load the WMATA ridership data. (2 points)

```{r}
rider_data <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/wmata_daily.csv")
```

### Task 6: Using `mutate()`, add a column called `rail_zscore` that is the z-score for rail ridership, calculated using the overall mean and standard deviation of all days. Save the result as `wmata_zscores`. (7 points)

```{r}
wmata_zscores <- rider_data |>
mutate(
  mean_rail = mean(rail),
  sd_rail= sd(rail),
  rail_zscore = (rail - mean_rail) / sd_rail
  
)

  

```

### Task 7: Rail ridership varies a lot by day of the week. Using `group_by()` and `mutate()`, add a column called `weekday_zscore` that calculates each day's rail z-score relative to other days with the same `weekday` (for example, a Sunday compared to other Sundays). Remember to `ungroup()` and save the result back to `wmata_zscores`. (8 points)

```{r}
wmata_zscores <- wmata_zscores |>
  mutate(
    weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE),
    month = floor_date(date, "month"),
    year = year(date)
  )

accidents <- wmata_zscores |>
  mutate(
    day_of_week = wday(date, label = TRUE),
    month = floor_date(date, "month"),
    year = year(date)
  )

# Check accident patterns by day of week
day_of_week_summary <- wmata_zscores |>
  group_by(weekday) |>
  summarize(
    avg_score = mean(rail),
    median_score = median(rail),
    max_score = max(rail),
    min_score = min(rail)
  )
  
```

### Task 8: Filter for days where the absolute value of `rail_zscore` is greater than 2, and separately for days where the absolute value of `weekday_zscore` is greater than 2. Arrange each so the most extreme days appear first. How many unusual days does each method find? (5 points)

```{r}
unusual_days <- wmata_zscores |>
  filter(abs(rail_zscore) > 2) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(rail_zscore)))
```

**How many unusual days does each method find?**


### Task 9: Write 2–3 sentences: How do the two lists of unusual days differ, and what story leads does each suggest? (8 points)

I didn't get the day specific one to work, but out of the entire list is shows the day that had the most unusually low rail days were Sundays. There's likely more traffic during the week rather than a Sunday which is usually the last day of the weekend. They also tend to occur in the winter.

Winter Weather Impacts WMATA Public Transit

## Part 3: Maryland Car Theft Rates (25 points)

Your editor has assigned you a story about car thefts in Maryland and wants you to find out which counties have the highest rates and which saw the biggest changes. The dataset contains car theft counts for Maryland counties in 2023 and 2024 along with population figures. Load the data from: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/md_car_thefts.csv`

### Task 10: Load the car thefts data. (2 points)

```{r}
md_car_thefts <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dwillis/jour405/refs/heads/main/data/md_car_thefts.csv")
```

### Task 11: Using `mutate()`, add two columns: `theft_rate`, the 2024 car theft rate per 10,000 residents, and `pct_change`, the percent change in thefts from 2023 to 2024. Save the result back to `md_car_thefts`. (10 points)

```{r}
md_car_thefts <- md_car_thefts |> mutate(theft_rate_2023=thefts_2023/population * 10000, theft_rate_2024=thefts_2024/population * 10000, pct_change=(thefts_2024-thefts_2023) /thefts_2023)
  
```


### Task 12: Show the five counties with the highest 2024 theft rate, the five with the largest percent increase, and the five with the largest percent decrease. (5 points)

```{r}
high_theft2024 <- md_car_thefts |>
  filter(abs(theft_rate_2024) > 21) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(theft_rate_2024)))

high_pct_change <- md_car_thefts |>
  filter(abs(pct_change) > 17.5) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(pct_change)))

high_pct_change <- md_car_thefts |>
  filter(abs(pct_change) > 17.5) |>
  arrange(asce(abs(pct_change)))




```

### Task 13: Write 2–3 sentences describing what these calculations reveal about car thefts in Maryland. What is the lede of a story based on your findings? (8 points)

These numbers tell me that generally there were more decreases in thefts across Maryland than increases. The three largest value percent changes were all negative, showing crime is seeing more county-specific decreases than increase.

Maryland Reports High Percentage Theft Drops in Multiple Counties From 2023 to 2024

## Part 4: Data Analysis Scenario (20 points)

A county parks department releases data showing that its 12 community swimming pools average 187 visitors per day during the summer season, with a standard deviation of 42 visitors across the pools' average daily attendance. Your editor suspects that a handful of pools are dramatically underperforming and wants a story. You also learn that the department's figures are based on a random sample of 60 days per pool rather than a complete count.

Write 4–5 sentences for each of the following questions:

### Question A: How would you use descriptive statistics and z-scores to identify which pools are genuinely underperforming, and why is that more useful than simply ranking pools by raw attendance? (10 points)

Z-scores would show us how many standard deviations away from the mean that certain pool locations would be reporting. Through this, we are able to tell where each location truly stands in comparison to the mean. By using other stats like the mean and median, we can discover where each location stands over a period of time. If you were to rank simply off of raw attendance over those 60 days, certain locations could be misrepresented due to their geographical location or other social factors. Certain pools could generally see more or less traffic throughout the day.


### Question B: The department collected its attendance figures using a random sample of 60 days per pool rather than tracking every day. What questions would you ask about the sample before relying on these figures for a story? What concerns would you raise in your story? (10 points)

I would first want to know how they picked the days when they sampled each location. Depending on their methods, they could have created sampling biases that don't accurately represent the average figures of each pool. If one location had 10 days chosen that were rainy, and another location had 3 rainy days chosen, naturally the one with less rainy days would likely have a higher population. Other things like holidays could also play a factor. Pools sampled on the 4th of July would naturally have a higher population sample for that day. I'd be concerned if every pool had a different 60-day sample.
